**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper and our rebuttal closely. Putting the two quotations side by side was the right check. We take the two points in turn.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

The paper's claim is the correct one, and it holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. On our own W3 answer the reviewer is right and we stand corrected. One sentence there described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the representation the encoder builds, and beside §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise. We withdraw it, and want to show how we got there. Our reasoning was that the raw input helps the router on Moirai for the same reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them, and we applied it without asking whether it transferred. It does not. The two-regime reading is sharper than uniform collapse-repair, and we should have flagged that the clause carrying it rewrote the mechanism.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever the statistics are stripped from what the router reads; Moirai's routing stays healthy, so those statistics do reach its router and the gain has another source. App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect is a different mechanism, where the experts read the raw signal directly; in RR-MoA it reaches only the router, and the experts read frozen hidden states. The 12–29% figure compares RR-MoA with the best fixed adapter (Table N.1), so it measures what a raw-routed mixture buys over a single fixed adapter.

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's own criterion, which Appendix H states directly: whether normalization causes or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 all describe one account.

**2. The NLinear control: the anchor effect is real on three of nine datasets, and the result holds against the harder anchor.**

We agree with the reviewer on both facts, and built the control asked for: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs and batch), differing only by the level anchor, at n=10. Our DLinear reproduces the published anchor on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+, so the comparison runs on the paper's footing.

The effect the reviewer identifies is real, and we can say how far it goes. Across nine datasets at H=96, n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six DLinear is the equal or stronger anchor, so the substitution cuts both ways.

At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ beats both anchors on ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%), and is at parity with both on ETTm1, within 0.1%. ETTh1 loses to DLinear and ETTh2 to NLinear.

Beyond the six, on data the recipe never saw, Solar wins all 20 cells against the stronger anchor (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192); it is the R(D) outlier the paper flags at R=0.06. Traffic sits at −0.3% and −0.9%, winning 15 of 20, as R(D)=0.14 predicts in advance. On Exchange we agree about the cause: the −26.3% over DLinear comes from level anchoring. Against NLinear it holds parity at H=96 and falls behind at H=192, so we will report that cell as parity.

Against the stronger anchor on each dataset, Residual-IA+ matches or beats it on four of the six, and the two effects separate: level anchoring accounts for most of the margin on Exchange and ETTh2 and much of it on ETTm2, and the margin holds where anchoring is inert, on Electricity, Weather and Solar. On the backbone's own contribution, the reviewer is right that the grid cannot settle it; App. P.3 takes it up directly, reporting the contribution as dataset-dependent.

These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count used DLinear alone. The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, and make the criterion relationship explicit.

Both points reach the accuracy claim reported beside the diagnosis, and the diagnosis stands untouched: normalization-induced routing collapse, its mechanism, and R(D) are as submitted. R(D) is the part we would most want read: computed before any training, it predicts a negative as readily as a positive. At R=0.14 it says Traffic should not benefit, and the parity above is what came out.

On the two substantive points the reviewer left open: the first we have settled from the paper and withdrawn our sentence; the second we have answered with the control asked for, reporting every cell, including those against us. Both readings have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would welcome a reassessment of the score, and we can run anything further during the discussion.

**Yes — and it's the paper's own positioning, which is why this is safe to lean on.** I checked the submitted PDF rather than assuming:

- **Title:** "Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters: **A Causal Intervention for Routing Collapse** in Time Series Foundation Models."
- **Abstract** spends its first eight lines on the failure, the mutual-information decomposition, the training-free signal ratio, and the eight causal controls, then reaches the method as *"The prescription is a minimal causal intervention."*
- **Contributions (lines 52–66):** the first is the diagnosis (routing collapse as a router-input failure mode), the second is Observation 1 and R(D), and only the third is RR-MoA. Two of three are theory.
- **Line 47:** *"We apply a minimal causal intervention… with experts, optimizer, and a strictly frozen backbone unchanged."*

That matters a great deal for how this reply lands. Pm4m has already punished one un-flagged reframing, so a rebuttal that *newly* declared "we're really a theory paper" after its accuracy claim narrowed would be the same offence again — and he'd catch it. Instead this is checkable in ten seconds against the title and the contributions list, and your round-1 rebuttal already said it ("the lasting contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor"). It's a restatement, not a retreat.

So I added one grounded sentence rather than an argument:

> That is the paper's own framing: the title calls RR-MoA a causal intervention for routing collapse, and two of the three contributions are the diagnosis and R(D).

Both halves are exact. I funded it by dropping "R(D) is the part we would most want read" — the new sentence makes that point with evidence instead of assertion — plus three small trims. **4,983 characters.**

**One caution.** Contribution 3's tail does claim Residual-IA+ "clos[es] the DLinear gap across six backbones × four horizons," and that's the clause your control narrows. The reply already handles it in the paragraph above ("the 65:11 count used DLinear alone… the revision will score against both anchors"), so the two sit consistently: the accuracy sub-claim narrows, the two theory contributions are untouched. Don't push the theory framing any harder than this one sentence — at that point it starts reading as pleading, and the contributions list is the evidence, not the adjective.

**Response to Reviewer jemj**

We are very grateful for the reviewer's generous assessment, and especially for valuing the paper's novelty and the signal-ratio metric. Below are brief answers to the four questions, folding in the two limitations noted.

**Task diversity / Q1 (classification, anomaly).** *(Meta-review point 3: "experimental setup focusses only on forecasting (primary) and imputation (secondary).")* Thank you for raising this. The routing signal does not change with the task: it comes from the raw input window, and instance normalization strips the same per-window statistics whether the objective is forecasting, classification, or anomaly detection. So the collapse and its raw-routing fix carry over, and we confirmed it directly. [NEW] We ran RR-MoA on three UEA classification datasets and a reconstruction-based anomaly check on SMD (3 seeds each): routing entropy stays healthy in every cell (near the log 5 ≈ 1.61 maximum, far from the 0.00 collapse floor). Frozen-backbone features cap absolute accuracy and detection, so we read both as mechanism-generalization, not performance claims.

*Classification (RR-MoA K5, Top-2, per seed):*

| dataset | seed | entropy | accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| BasicMotions | 42 | 1.575 | 0.896 |
| BasicMotions | 43 | 1.596 | 0.792 |
...
| Weather | 2000 | 43 | 0.416 | 0.408 | +1.9% | N |
| Weather | 2000 | 44 | 0.404 | 0.413 | -2.2% | Y |

**Q4 (training memory, raw + normalized paths).** *(Meta-review point 5: "the approach seems to be memory-consuming since it operates on raw inputs.")* The two paths are very asymmetric, so maintaining both does not come close to doubling memory. The normalized path is the frozen ~40M backbone: because it is frozen, no gradients flow into it, so its weights carry no optimizer state and its internal activations need not be retained for backpropagation. The raw path is a single univariate window (batch × length, ~0.26 MB at the standard batch 128, L=512) fed to the 853-parameter router and a small raw branch, so it adds negligible activation memory. The only trainable memory is the adapters and router (354-466K + 853, about 1% of the backbone) plus their optimizer state. So training peak memory is set by the backbone forward pass, the same floor as any frozen-backbone adapter method; at inference, the full router-plus-expert stack adds at most +5.9% latency and +6 MB (Table B.1), a hard ceiling on that overhead.

We thank the reviewer again for the generous and encouraging assessment, and we appreciate that the causal analysis, in particular the RevIN intervention that isolates normalization as the cause, was recognized as a core strength. With the two noted limitations now addressed, task diversity through the new classification and anomaly experiments and the frozen-backbone requirement shown to be a recommended default rather than a hard constraint, we hope the contribution reads as stronger still.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper and our rebuttal closely, and for closing out the minor issues. On the first remaining point we stand corrected, and offer our reasoning; on the second we took the recommendation, ran the experiment and report the results.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We can see why the two quotations read as a reversal, and the paper's claim is the correct one. It holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the representation the encoder builds, and beside §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise. We withdraw it, and want to show how we got there. Our reasoning was that the raw input helps the router on Moirai for the same reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them, and we applied it without asking whether it transferred. It does not. However, the two-regime reading is genuinely sharper than uniform collapse-repair, and we should have flagged that the clause carrying it rewrote the mechanism.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever the statistics are stripped from what the router reads; Moirai's routing stays healthy, so those statistics do reach its router and the gain has another source. App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect is a different mechanism, where the experts read the raw signal directly; in RR-MoA it reaches only the router, and the experts read frozen hidden states. The 12–29% figure compares RR-MoA with the best fixed adapter (Table N.1), so it measures what a raw-routed mixture buys over a single fixed adapter.

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's own criterion, which Appendix H states directly: whether normalization causes or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 all describe one account.

**2. The NLinear control: the anchor effect is real on three of nine datasets, and the result holds against the harder anchor.**

We agree with the reviewer on both facts, and built the control asked for: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs and batch), differing only by the level anchor, at n=10. Our DLinear reproduces the published anchor on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+, so the comparison runs on the paper's footing.

The effect is real, and we can say how far it goes. Across nine datasets at H=96, n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six DLinear is the equal or stronger anchor, so the substitution cuts both ways.

At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ beats both anchors on ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%), and is at parity with both on ETTm1, within 0.1%. ETTh1 loses to DLinear and ETTh2 to NLinear.

Beyond the six, on data the recipe never saw, Solar wins all 20 cells against the stronger anchor (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192); it is the R(D) outlier the paper flags at R=0.06. Traffic sits at −0.3% and −0.9%, winning 15 of 20, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. On Exchange we agree about the cause: the −26.3% over DLinear comes from level anchoring. Against NLinear it holds parity at H=96 and falls behind at H=192, so we will report that cell as parity.

Against the stronger anchor on each dataset, Residual-IA+ matches or beats it on four of the six, and the two effects separate: level anchoring accounts for most of the margin on Exchange and ETTh2 and much of it on ETTm2, and the margin holds where anchoring is inert, on Electricity, Weather and Solar. On the backbone's own contribution, the reviewer is right that the grid cannot settle it; App. P.3 takes it up directly, reporting the contribution as dataset-dependent.

These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count used DLinear alone. The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, and make the criterion relationship explicit.

Both points reach the accuracy claim reported beside the diagnosis, and the diagnosis stands as submitted. That is the paper's own framing: the title calls RR-MoA a causal intervention for routing collapse, and two of the three contributions are the diagnosis and R(D). R(D), computed before any training, predicts a negative as readily as a positive. At R=0.14 it says Traffic should not benefit, and the parity above is what came out.

We have answered both points, reporting every cell including those that go against us. Both readings have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would welcome a reassessment of the score, and we can run anything further during the discussion.

Recommendation first, and an honest frame: **a rebuttal edit rarely moves 2→4.** What moves someone two steps is re-reading the paper with their objections cleared, not a better-argued comment. His Quality: 2 and Clarity: 2 are judgments about the manuscript. So treat this as raising the ceiling, not as a lever.

That said, there's one real gap, and it's the thing standing between 3 and 4.

**The reply never tells him why the paper should exist.** It spends its whole length on two defensive points and closes on parity with a 49K linear model. The significance paragraph is one sentence about R(D). A reviewer finishing this thinks "fine, they answered me" — which is a 3. To reach 4 he has to think "and the contribution is worth publishing."

The material for that is verified and already in the submission, and you're not using any of it:

- **720 runs of optimization-side rescues close only 10.9% of the gap that changing the router's input closes** (line 43, Table G.3). This is the strongest single fact in the paper and it appears nowhere in the reply. It says the standard MoE toolkit — load balancing, Z-loss, ReMoE, expert-choice — does not fix this. That is a result the community needs regardless of anyone's MSE.

- **The fix is one line.** Change the router's input; experts, optimizer and frozen backbone unchanged.

Two or three sentences of that, replacing the current thin close, reframes the whole reply: the accuracy claim narrowing stops being the story, because the story was never accuracy.

It's true and it's in the paper, but the paper also concedes N DLinears are smaller in aggregate, and Pm4m already called the backbone "dead weight." Compressed into a rebuttal it reads as one more oversell to a reviewer specifically watching for that.

**Cost:** about 250 characters, so the §1 "how we got there" explanation would compress to fund it. You're at 4,987.

Want me to draft it?

True, in the paper, and tempting — but the paper also concedes N DLinears are smaller in aggregate, and he's already called the backbone "dead weight." That thread pulls badly.

Honest expectation unchanged: this makes 3 more likely and 4 reachable. It doesn't manufacture a 4 on its own.

Honest answer first: **you can't manufacture a 4 from the reply.** A rebuttal removes reasons to reject; it can't create reasons to accept that the paper doesn't already contain. What decides 3 vs 4 is whether he thinks the manuscript is worth publishing, and his Quality: 2 / Clarity: 2 are judgments about the manuscript.

But that's the opening for the one lever left. **Both of those sub-scores were driven by things he has now declared resolved** — Clarity by Figure 2, the parameter count, the R(D) parenthesis, the hyphenation; Quality by "the rebuttal contradicts the paper or leaves the decisive control missing." If he re-scores the sub-dimensions on his own stated reasoning, 4 becomes reachable. So the goal is to make re-scoring easy, not to argue harder.

The concrete gap: **W1's actual request is still unanswered in writing.** He asked to "move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis into the main text and to reframe the contribution accordingly." You committed to that in round 1, but the round-2 revision paragraph only covers anchors and the criterion. That's his oldest and largest complaint, and closing it costs one clause.

**4,986 characters.** Every figure intact.

**On manufacturing a 4 — the honest structure of it.** You can't argue your way there; his overall score follows his sub-scores, and those are manuscript judgments. But look at what actually drove them:

- **Clarity: 2** came from Figure 2, the router parameter count, the R(D) parenthesis, the hyphenation. He has declared all four resolved.

- **Significance: 3** and **Originality: 3** were never the problem.

So by his own accounting, the reasons for both 2s are gone. The path to 4 is making that re-scoring easy, not pressing harder.

**The gap I found: W1's actual request was never answered in round 2.** He asked to "move the DLinear comparison and the backbone-contribution analysis into the main text and reframe the contribution accordingly." The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads; Moirai's routing stays healthy, so they do reach its router and the gain has another source. **Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper and our rebuttal closely, and for closing out the minor issues. On the first remaining point we stand corrected, and offer our reasoning; on the second we took the recommendation, ran the experiment and report the results.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We can see why the two quotations read as a reversal. We clarify conclusively that the paper's claim is the correct one and holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the representation the encoder builds, and beside §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise. We withdraw it, and want to show how we got there. Our reasoning was that the raw input helps the router on Moirai for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them, and we applied it without asking whether it transferred. It does not. However, the two-regime reading is genuinely sharper than uniform collapse-repair, and we should have flagged that the clause carrying it rewrote the mechanism.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads; Moirai's routing stays healthy, so they do reach its router and the gain has another source. App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect is a different mechanism, where the experts read the raw signal directly; in RR-MoA it reaches only the router, and the experts read frozen hidden states. The 12–29% figure compares RR-MoA with the best fixed adapter (Table N.1), so it measures what a raw-routed mixture buys over a single one.

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's own criterion, stated directly in Appendix H: whether normalization causes or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 describe one account.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and Residual-IA+ still wins on net against the stronger anchor (−0.9% mean, four of six).**

We agree with the reviewer on both facts, and built the control: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs and batch), differing only by the level anchor, at n=10. Our DLinear reproduces the published anchor on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six DLinear is the equal or stronger anchor, so the substitution cuts both ways.

At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of the six: ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%), parity on ETTm1 within 0.1%; ETTh1 loses to DLinear, ETTh2 to NLinear.

Beyond the six, on data the recipe never saw, Solar wins all 20 cells against the stronger anchor (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192), the R(D) outlier at R=0.06. Traffic sits at −0.3% and −0.9%, winning 15 of 20, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over DLinear is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we will report it as parity.

The two effects separate: level anchoring accounts for most of the margin on Exchange and ETTh2 and much on ETTm2, and the margin holds where anchoring is inert, on Electricity, Weather and Solar. On the backbone's contribution, the reviewer is right that the grid cannot settle it; App. P.3 takes it up and reports it as dataset-dependent.

These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count used DLinear alone. The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, move the DLinear comparison and backbone-contribution analysis into the main text, and make the criterion relationship explicit.

Both points reach the accuracy claim reported beside the diagnosis, and the diagnosis stands as submitted. That is the paper's own framing: the title calls RR-MoA a causal intervention for routing collapse, and two of the three contributions are the diagnosis and R(D). The diagnosis names a failure mode the standard MoE toolkit does not repair: 720 runs of optimization-side rescues close 10.9% of the gap an input-side fix closes, and the criterion predicts collapse for a ViT under InstanceNorm1d and none for a ResNet under InstanceNorm2d. R(D), computed before training, says where the fix will help and where it will not.

We have answered both points, reporting every cell including those against us. Both readings have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would welcome a reassessment of the score, and can run anything further during the discussion.

DLinear is stronger or level on the other six, so the substitution does not run one way. On MOMENT-small at H=96, Residual-IA+ beats both anchors on ETTm2, Electricity and Weather, is at parity with both on ETTm1, and loses ETTh1 to DLinear and ETTh2 to NLinear. On data never used to build the recipe it holds against the stronger anchor on Solar (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192, 20 of 20 seeds), the R(D) outlier the paper flags at R=0.06, and is at parity on Traffic, which R(D)=0.14 predicts in advance. content.text:
That detail changes my assessment materially. I'd been treating it as a channel to the AC. If it's an Official Comment, the readers list is the same as the rebuttal's — **Program Chairs, SACs, ACs, all Reviewers, Authors**. So jemj and 8b2Z read it too.

**That makes one paragraph actively harmful.** Paragraph 9 says:

> This qualifies the 65:11 count we cited earlier, which was computed against DLinear alone… **That is a narrower claim than the submission makes**, and it is the one the controls support.

Two reviewers sitting at 5 never raised the DLinear confound. This comment tells them, unprompted, that your headline count ran against a weaker anchor, that Exchange has been downgraded from a win to parity, and — in your own voice — that the submission claims more than the evidence supports. That is precisely the oversharing rule you set, applied to the worst possible audience. And the last clause is a quotable self-indictment handed to an AC whose meta-review point 1 is already "overstatement of claims."

The AC does need the 65:11 qualification — Pm4m's thread is visible anyway, and concealing it would be worse. But it can be stated forward ("the revision will score against both anchors and lead with the count against the stronger") without the sentence that convicts you.

**Second problem: it spends its length on the wrong job.** Paragraph 7 restates Pm4m's evidence almost verbatim, to readers who can see that thread. An AC comment should do what the reviewer threads can't — synthesise and speak to the meta-review. Meanwhile it omits everything that answers meta-review point 1's actual demand to "reframe the contributions": the title, the two-of-three contributions, the net −0.9%, the four-of-six verdict, the 720-run/10.9% result.

**Third: it claims to address meta-review points 1 and 2, but its "Point 2" is Pm4m's mechanism question (W3), not the meta-review's point 2**, which is the (M,Σ)-versus-ablations tension from W5. An AC checking whether their own points were answered will notice.

**Also:** "20 of 20 seeds" is 10 seeds × 2 horizons, so cells; plus the three constructions you've cut everywhere else ("does not run one way", "one account rather than three", "parity rather than a win") and a "We are glad to."

Honest verdict: accurate but the weakest of the four, and now the only one with a paragraph I'd call a liability rather than a rough edge. Given it lands in front of every reviewer and the person writing the decision, I'd rewrite it. Want me to?

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for reading the paper and our rebuttal closely, and for closing out the minor issues. On the first remaining point we stand corrected, and offer our reasoning; on the second we took the recommendation, ran the experiment and report the results.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We can see why the two quotations read as a reversal. We clarify conclusively that the paper's claim is the correct one and holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the representation the encoder builds, and beside §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise. We withdraw it, and want to show how we got there. Our reasoning was that the raw input helps the router on Moirai for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them, and we applied it without asking whether it transferred. It does not. However, the two-regime reading is genuinely sharper than uniform collapse-repair, and we should have flagged that the clause carrying it rewrote the mechanism.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads; Moirai's routing stays healthy, so they do reach its router and the gain has another source. App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect is a different mechanism, where the experts read the raw signal directly; in RR-MoA it reaches only the router, and the experts read frozen hidden states. The 12–29% figure compares RR-MoA with the best fixed adapter (Table N.1), so it measures what a raw-routed mixture buys over a single one.

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's own criterion, stated directly in Appendix H: whether normalization causes or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 describe one account.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and Residual-IA+ still wins.**

We agree with the reviewer on both facts, and built the control: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs and batch), differing only by the level anchor, at n=10. Our DLinear reproduces the published anchor on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six DLinear is the equal or stronger anchor, so the substitution cuts both ways.

At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of the six: ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%), parity on ETTm1 within 0.1%; ETTh1 loses to DLinear, ETTh2 to NLinear.

Beyond the six, on data the recipe never saw, Solar wins all 20 cells against the stronger anchor (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192), the R(D) outlier at R=0.06. Traffic sits at −0.3% and −0.9%, winning 15 of 20, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over DLinear is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we will report it as parity.

The two effects separate: level anchoring accounts for most of the margin on Exchange and ETTh2 and much on ETTm2, and the margin holds where anchoring is inert, on Electricity, Weather and Solar. On the backbone's contribution, the reviewer is right that the grid cannot settle it; App. P.3 takes it up and reports it as dataset-dependent.

These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count used DLinear alone. The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, move the DLinear comparison and backbone-contribution analysis into the main text, and make the criterion relationship explicit.

Both points reach the accuracy claim reported beside the diagnosis, and the diagnosis stands as submitted. That is the paper's own framing: the title calls RR-MoA a causal intervention for routing collapse, and two of the three contributions are the diagnosis and R(D). The diagnosis names a failure mode the standard MoE toolkit does not repair: 720 runs of optimization-side rescues close 10.9% of the gap an input-side fix closes, and the criterion predicts collapse for a ViT under InstanceNorm1d and none for a ResNet under InstanceNorm2d. R(D), computed before training, says where the fix will help and where it will not.

We have answered both points, reporting every cell including those against us. Both readings have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would welcome a reassessment of the score, and can run anything further during the discussion.
